raw_segments.text: Father Wolf waited till his cubs could run a little, and then on the night of the pack
meeting took them, and Mowgli and Mother Wolf to the council rock a hilltop, covered with
stones and boulders where a hundred wolves could hide.
Aikla, the great gray lone wolf, who led all the pack by strength and cunning, lay out
at full length on his rock, and below him sat forty or more wolves of every size and
color, from badger-colored veterans who could handle a buck alone to young black three-year-olds
The lone wolf had led them for a year now.
He had fallen twice into a wolf trap in his youth, and once he had been beaten and left
for dead, so he knew the manners and customs of men.
There was very little talking at the rock.
The cubs tumbled over each other in the center of the circle where their mothers and fathers
sat, and now and again a senior wolf would go quietly up to a cub, look at him carefully,
and return to his place on noiseless feet.
Sometimes a mother would push her cub far out into the moonlight to be sure that he
Aikla from his rock would cry, you know the law, you know the law, look well, oh wolves.
And the anxious mothers would take up the call, look, look well, oh wolves.
